knowledge_fragments.content: Understanding the complex pathophysiology of SH-OH in primary autonomic dysfunction is the first step to promoting future research aimed at developing a definitive treatment of this disorder. However, it is important to remember that autonomic dysfunction can have many causes and is usually not due to a primary disorder such as MSA or pure autonomic failure. Disorders such as these can be helpful as they provide a framework for understanding the complexity of this disease. In the next section, we review current methods and techniques for evaluation and treatment of autonomic dysfunction with SH-OH.
knowledge_fragments.title: Syndrome of Supine Hypertension with Orthostatic Hypotension: Pathophysiology and Clinical Approach. > PHYSIOLOGY OF ORTHOSTATIC POSTURE > Development of Supine Hypertension in Autonomic Dysfunction

knowledge_fragments.content: Though there are many potential secondary causes of autonomic dysfunction, dysautonomia with impaired blood pressure regulation is more typical of primary autonomic dysfunction. Primary autonomic disorders include MSA and pure autonomic failure. It is important to be familiar with the pathophysiology and clinical picture of these conditions in order to better understand the development of SH-OH.
knowledge_fragments.title: Syndrome of Supine Hypertension with Orthostatic Hypotension: Pathophysiology and Clinical Approach. > PHYSIOLOGY OF ORTHOSTATIC POSTURE > Autonomic Failure

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 7-year-old Caucasian boy presented with multiple system issues including autonomic dysfunction, gastroesophageal reflux, gastroparesis, nocturnal hypoventilation, and metabolic abnormalities such as elevated lactate and pyruvate levels. At baseline, he exhibited a sleep-related breathing disorder with hypoventilation, characterized by hypercapnia with end tidal carbon dioxide levels (EtCO2) exceeding 50 torr for more than 25% of the measured sleep time. A nocturnal polysomnography study conducted immediately before an acute decompensation period showed continued hypoventilation with hypoxemia (average oxygen levels at 88%, with a nadir of 73% without breathing support) and hypercapnia (EtCO2: 49–65), along with an average of 3 central apneas per hour. Noninvasive ventilation was initiated using Bilevel Positive Airway Pressure (BiPap) at settings of 12/6 cmH2O to address the sleep disturbances. Prior to acute respiratory decompensation, he was at his medical baseline, active, and attending school. His mother reported headaches associated with elevated blood pressure (averaging 135/88: stage 2 hypertension), leading to the prescription of metoprolol at a dose of 25 m

knowledge_fragments.content: The presence of SH in a patient with orthostatic intolerance secondary to autonomic dysfunction greatly complicates the management of that patient. Additionally, the etiology of this SH can be difficult to ascertain. In fact, the physiology behind the development of SH in patients with autonomic failure differs between diseases, but there appears to be an association between the severity of SH and the degree of OH.
knowledge_fragments.title: Syndrome of Supine Hypertension with Orthostatic Hypotension: Pathophysiology and Clinical Approach. > PHYSIOLOGY OF ORTHOSTATIC POSTURE > Development of Supine Hypertension in Autonomic Dysfunction

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 27-year-old male with a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus and extensive dysautonomia was admitted to the hospital. He presented with diabetic retinopathy. On physical examination, he had sinus tachycardia with a pulse rate of 109 beats/min. Enlarged lymph nodes were palpable on the left side of the neck and groin, and a nodule was detected in the left testis. Neurological examination showed paresthesia in the distal extremities and absent Achilles-tendon reflexes. The patient had various autonomic symptoms, including orthostatic intolerance, dry eyes and mouth, dry skin, alternating loose stools and constipation, neurogenic bladder, and erectile dysfunction. Laboratory tests indicated normal serum levels of calcium and ACE, and a moderately elevated glycated hemoglobin level (7.5% [normal range 6.2%]). Antibodies against gAChR were absent. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed slightly elevated total protein levels (52 mg/dL [normal range 40 mg/dL]), with normal cell count, glucose, ACE, and immunoglobulin G index. Nerve conduction studies were unremarkable. A head-up tilt test indicated neurally mediated syncope, with systolic blood pressure dropping from 100 to 80
knowledge_fragments.title: Case report: Neurosarcoidosis with autonomic dysfunction

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A novel variant mutation of transthyretin Ile73Val-related amyloidotic polyneuropathy in Taiwanese.. Salient findings: symptoms and signs of sensory motor polyneuropathy; early gastrointestinal autonomic dysfunction; orthostatic hypotension; cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction; impaired sudomotor activity; gastrointestinal dysfunction; painful neuropathy. Confirmed diagnosis: Familial amyloidotic polyneuropathy (FAP). Differential diagnosis includes: Familial amyloidotic polyneuropathy (FAP); FAP; amyloidotic polyneuropathy; axonal sensory-motor polyneuropathy; amyloidotic restrictive cardiomyopathy.
knowledge_fragments.title: Case report: Familial amyloidotic polyneuropathy (FAP)

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 69-year-old male patient was admitted to the hospital due to recurrent episodes of fainting and difficulty in urination over the past 2 years. He had a history of constipation for 10 years. One year before admission, he was prescribed midodrine hydrochloride, amezinium metilsulfate, and droxidopa, which alleviated the fainting episodes, though he continued to experience difficulty standing up without feeling dizzy. He had a history of pulmonary, skin, and ocular conditions. Upon admission, he presented with various autonomic symptoms, including low blood pressure upon standing, high blood pressure while lying down, dizziness, fainting, alternating between loose stools and constipation, and difficulty in urination. Additionally, he reported a burning sensation extending from his navel to the outer side of his lower leg and big toe.. Confirmed diagnosis: Neurosarcoidosis with autonomic dysfunction associated with anti-ganglionic acetylcholine receptor antibodies. Differential diagnosis includes: Neurosarcoidosis with autonomic dysfunction associated with anti-ganglionic acetylcholine receptor antibodies.
knowledge_fragments.title: Case report: Neurosarcoidosis with autonomic dysfunction associated with anti-ganglionic acetylcholine receptor antibodies

knowledge_fragments.content: Tables 4 and 5 summarize guidelines for managing and reducing cardiovascular risk and clinical management strategies for autonomic dysfunction. A clinical practice guideline, formulated by an international panel in 2021, concluded that although there was good consensus among the expert panel, evidence-based recommendations for the management of autonomic dysfunction are limited, and based largely on expert opinion. There appears to be no single strategy for management used in clinical practice. Rather, a comprehensive approach combining preventive strategies, non-pharmacologic interventions, and pharmacologic management has been recommended. Newer options for managing autonomic dysfunction involve spinal cord stimulation, and these studies are summarized in Table 7.
knowledge_fragments.title: Evaluation and management of autonomic functions in patients with spinal cord injury: A scoping review. > Results > Study sample and characteristics > Management of cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction

knowledge_fragments.content: The articles reviewed were grouped according to whether they were narrative reviews focusing on the pathophysiology and clinical manifestations of cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction (Table 2), measurement (Table 3) of autonomic symptoms, reviews focusing on the management (Table 4) or guidelines regarding the documentation and management of autonomic dysfunction (Table 5), original research articles, including case studies, concerned with measurement and management of autonomic dysfunction (Table 6), and systematic or scoping reviews of interventions to manage autonomic symptoms or to attenuate cardiovascular risk (Table 7). Detailed summaries of these articles are documented in the respective Tables, organized according to date.
knowledge_fragments.title: Evaluation and management of autonomic functions in patients with spinal cord injury: A scoping review. > Results > Study sample and characteristics

knowledge_fragments.content: The management of autonomic dysfunction following SCI is primarily guided by expert consensus-based clinical recommendations (Table 5). However, there is no definitive treatment for preventing or managing cardiovascular complications such as AD and OH. Further, existing management guidelines are largely based on low-quality evidence.
knowledge_fragments.title: Evaluation and management of autonomic functions in patients with spinal cord injury: A scoping review. > Discussion > Management of cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 7-year-old Caucasian boy presented with multiple system issues including autonomic dysfunction, gastroesophageal reflux, gastroparesis, nocturnal hypoventilation, and metabolic abnormalities such as elevated lactate and pyruvate levels. At baseline, he exhibited a sleep-related breathing disorder with hypoventilation, characterized by hypercapnia with end tidal carbon dioxide levels (EtCO2) exceeding 50 torr for more than 25% of the measured sleep time. A nocturnal polysomnography study conducted immediately before an acute decompensation period showed continued hypoventilation with hypoxemia (average oxygen levels at 88%, with a nadir of 73% without breathing support) and hypercapnia (EtCO2: 49–65), along with an average of 3 central apneas per hour. Noninvasive ventilation was initiated using Bilevel Positive Airway Pressure (BiPap) at settings of 12/6 cmH2O to address the sleep disturbances. Prior to acute respiratory decompensation, he was at his medical baseline, active, and attending school. His mother reported headaches associated with elevated blood pressure (averaging 135/88: stage 2 hypertension), leading to the prescription of metoprolol at a dose of 25 m

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A novel variant mutation of transthyretin Ile73Val-related amyloidotic polyneuropathy in Taiwanese.. Salient findings: symptoms and signs of sensory motor polyneuropathy; early gastrointestinal autonomic dysfunction; orthostatic hypotension; cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction; impaired sudomotor activity; gastrointestinal dysfunction; painful neuropathy. Confirmed diagnosis: Familial amyloidotic polyneuropathy (FAP). Differential diagnosis includes: Familial amyloidotic polyneuropathy (FAP); FAP; amyloidotic polyneuropathy; axonal sensory-motor polyneuropathy; amyloidotic restrictive cardiomyopathy.
knowledge_fragments.title: Case report: Familial amyloidotic polyneuropathy (FAP)

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 27-year-old male with a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus and extensive dysautonomia was admitted to the hospital. He presented with diabetic retinopathy. On physical examination, he had sinus tachycardia with a pulse rate of 109 beats/min. Enlarged lymph nodes were palpable on the left side of the neck and groin, and a nodule was detected in the left testis. Neurological examination showed paresthesia in the distal extremities and absent Achilles-tendon reflexes. The patient had various autonomic symptoms, including orthostatic intolerance, dry eyes and mouth, dry skin, alternating loose stools and constipation, neurogenic bladder, and erectile dysfunction. Laboratory tests indicated normal serum levels of calcium and ACE, and a moderately elevated glycated hemoglobin level (7.5% [normal range 6.2%]). Antibodies against gAChR were absent. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed slightly elevated total protein levels (52 mg/dL [normal range 40 mg/dL]), with normal cell count, glucose, ACE, and immunoglobulin G index. Nerve conduction studies were unremarkable. A head-up tilt test indicated neurally mediated syncope, with systolic blood pressure dropping from 100 to 80
knowledge_fragments.title: Case report: Neurosarcoidosis with autonomic dysfunction

knowledge_fragments.content: Understanding the complex pathophysiology of SH-OH in primary autonomic dysfunction is the first step to promoting future research aimed at developing a definitive treatment of this disorder. However, it is important to remember that autonomic dysfunction can have many causes and is usually not due to a primary disorder such as MSA or pure autonomic failure. Disorders such as these can be helpful as they provide a framework for understanding the complexity of this disease. In the next section, we review current methods and techniques for evaluation and treatment of autonomic dysfunction with SH-OH.
knowledge_fragments.title: Syndrome of Supine Hypertension with Orthostatic Hypotension: Pathophysiology and Clinical Approach. > PHYSIOLOGY OF ORTHOSTATIC POSTURE > Development of Supine Hypertension in Autonomic Dysfunction

knowledge_fragments.content: Though there are many potential secondary causes of autonomic dysfunction, dysautonomia with impaired blood pressure regulation is more typical of primary autonomic dysfunction. Primary autonomic disorders include MSA and pure autonomic failure. It is important to be familiar with the pathophysiology and clinical picture of these conditions in order to better understand the development of SH-OH.
knowledge_fragments.title: Syndrome of Supine Hypertension with Orthostatic Hypotension: Pathophysiology and Clinical Approach. > PHYSIOLOGY OF ORTHOSTATIC POSTURE > Autonomic Failure

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 69-year-old male patient was admitted to the hospital due to recurrent episodes of fainting and difficulty in urination over the past 2 years. He had a history of constipation for 10 years. One year before admission, he was prescribed midodrine hydrochloride, amezinium metilsulfate, and droxidopa, which alleviated the fainting episodes, though he continued to experience difficulty standing up without feeling dizzy. He had a history of pulmonary, skin, and ocular conditions. Upon admission, he presented with various autonomic symptoms, including low blood pressure upon standing, high blood pressure while lying down, dizziness, fainting, alternating between loose stools and constipation, and difficulty in urination. Additionally, he reported a burning sensation extending from his navel to the outer side of his lower leg and big toe.. Confirmed diagnosis: Neurosarcoidosis with autonomic dysfunction associated with anti-ganglionic acetylcholine receptor antibodies. Differential diagnosis includes: Neurosarcoidosis with autonomic dysfunction associated with anti-ganglionic acetylcholine receptor antibodies.
knowledge_fragments.title: Case report: Neurosarcoidosis with autonomic dysfunction associated with anti-ganglionic acetylcholine receptor antibodies

knowledge_fragments.content: Tables 4 and 5 summarize guidelines for managing and reducing cardiovascular risk and clinical management strategies for autonomic dysfunction. A clinical practice guideline, formulated by an international panel in 2021, concluded that although there was good consensus among the expert panel, evidence-based recommendations for the management of autonomic dysfunction are limited, and based largely on expert opinion. There appears to be no single strategy for management used in clinical practice. Rather, a comprehensive approach combining preventive strategies, non-pharmacologic interventions, and pharmacologic management has been recommended. Newer options for managing autonomic dysfunction involve spinal cord stimulation, and these studies are summarized in Table 7.
knowledge_fragments.title: Evaluation and management of autonomic functions in patients with spinal cord injury: A scoping review. > Results > Study sample and characteristics > Management of cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction

knowledge_fragments.content: The presence of SH in a patient with orthostatic intolerance secondary to autonomic dysfunction greatly complicates the management of that patient. Additionally, the etiology of this SH can be difficult to ascertain. In fact, the physiology behind the development of SH in patients with autonomic failure differs between diseases, but there appears to be an association between the severity of SH and the degree of OH.
knowledge_fragments.title: Syndrome of Supine Hypertension with Orthostatic Hypotension: Pathophysiology and Clinical Approach. > PHYSIOLOGY OF ORTHOSTATIC POSTURE > Development of Supine Hypertension in Autonomic Dysfunction

knowledge_fragments.content: The articles reviewed were grouped according to whether they were narrative reviews focusing on the pathophysiology and clinical manifestations of cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction (Table 2), measurement (Table 3) of autonomic symptoms, reviews focusing on the management (Table 4) or guidelines regarding the documentation and management of autonomic dysfunction (Table 5), original research articles, including case studies, concerned with measurement and management of autonomic dysfunction (Table 6), and systematic or scoping reviews of interventions to manage autonomic symptoms or to attenuate cardiovascular risk (Table 7). Detailed summaries of these articles are documented in the respective Tables, organized according to date.
knowledge_fragments.title: Evaluation and management of autonomic functions in patients with spinal cord injury: A scoping review. > Results > Study sample and characteristics

knowledge_fragments.content: The management of autonomic dysfunction following SCI is primarily guided by expert consensus-based clinical recommendations (Table 5). However, there is no definitive treatment for preventing or managing cardiovascular complications such as AD and OH. Further, existing management guidelines are largely based on low-quality evidence.
knowledge_fragments.title: Evaluation and management of autonomic functions in patients with spinal cord injury: A scoping review. > Discussion > Management of cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction

tree.case_summary:
A 33-year-old male construction worker is brought to the emergency department with acute confusion after being found unconscious at his worksite. His medical history includes seizure disorder and schizophrenia, for which he takes haloperidol. He underwent an appendectomy two months ago. On examination, his vital signs show: temperature 105°F (40.6°C), blood pressure 120/84 mmHg, heart rate 150/min, respiratory rate 19/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. The patient is confused and non-communicative, with sweat-soaked clothing. While he shows no clear focal neurologic deficits, he lacks purposeful movement of his extremities. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Anticholinergic toxicity
B. Exertional heat stroke
C. Malignant hyperthermia
D. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
E. Central nervous system infection
F. Drug-induced hyperthermia
G. Septic shock
H. Nonexertional heat stroke
I. Thyroid storm
J. Status epilepticus

excluded_candidates: Seizure disorder: patient's known history, but current presentation suggests other acute causes
Schizophrenia: patient's known history, but current presentation suggests other acute causes
Post-operative complications: patient underwent appendectomy two months ago, but current presentation suggests other acute causes
